To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

psoriasis may result from a defect in the adenine 3′ 5′-monophosphate (AMP) mediated cascade, that the defect is in the adenylcyclase-cyclic AMP system and that this system is not functioning properly in the epidermal cell of the psoriatic lesion.
epidermal cells from patients with psoriasis have an increased rate of division, and beta adrenergics inhibit epidermal cell proliferation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the hypothesis that psoriasis may result from a polygenic, environmentally induced defect in the epidermal cyclic AMP cascade.
the possible role of cyclic AMP as a mediator of epidermal cell growth and differentiation.
the hypothesis that the adenyl cyclases of the epidermis, and perhaps of all cells, are subject to a negative feedback control by a protein kinase which in turn is regulated by cyclic AMP.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
psoriasis appears to be a polygenic, environmentally induced defect in a chalone system, and that the epidermis is the target of the disease.
the adenyl cyclases of the epidermis and dermis are defective in their ability to respond to the beta adrenergics.
psoriasis is a polygenic-environ- mentally induced defect in the cyclic AMP cascade.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the epidermal chalone mechanism is defective in psoriasis.
the cyclic AMP dependent protein kinase system appears to be a normal regulator of epidermal cell proliferation.
psoriasis may represent a polygenetic-environmentally induced disorder in the adenyl-cyclase-cyclic AMP dependent cascade.
The main takeaway from our work is that
psoriasis is not a disease of the immune system.
psoriasis may represent an inherited defect of a chalone mechanism.
the cyclic AMP system is involved in the regulation of epidermal cell proliferation.
